learnerStatement: Simulated learner. This review finds problems; it is not evidence that anyone learned.
learnerBoundary: Everyday numeracy, simple charts, comparing numbers and familiar household objects; no domain-specific theory assumed.

observations.prediction: Selected 90% and locked the yield prediction for 1.80 g aspirin collected from 2.00 g salicylic acid, with theoretical aspirin output 2.61 g.
observations.exploration: Activated grams-to-moles and moles-to-aspirin-grams stages. The diagram showed 2.00 divided by 138.12 equals 0.01448 mol, then multiplied by 180.16 to give 2.61 g possible aspirin. At 0.50 g collected yield was 19%; setting 1.80 g gave 69%; changing collected mass to 2.00 g gave 77%.
observations.reveal: The reveal corrected the original answer to 69% and explained actual product divided by possible product, not starting reactant mass. It used the one-to-one mole conversion and different molar masses. It returned in prose to the visited 1.80 g scenario while the live slider remained at 2.00 g.
observations.visual: Inspected the inline dark 1257 by 936 screenshot after both conversion stages at 0.50 g collected. A grey 2.00 g input bar, a longer dashed 2.61 g possible-product bar and a short pink actual-product bar shared a gram scale. The two conversion equations were readable.
observations.isolation: No-history evaluation preview banner present. Visible trust count ignored.
observations.reference: Own CUA tab 543884163 snapshots and inspected inline screenshot; no screenshot file saved.

prediction.reason: The question targets a plausible but wrong mass-ratio denominator.
prediction.evidence: Selected 1.80 divided by 2.00, or 90%, despite the supplied theoretical product mass.

interaction.reason: Conversion stages and collected-mass changes expose the correct reference quantity.
interaction.evidence: Even 2.00 g collected is only 77% of the possible 2.61 g.

payoff.reason: The reveal explains the denominator using amount conversion and product molar mass.
payoff.evidence: The one-to-one 0.01448 mol relation produces a different mass for aspirin.

clarity.reason: The bars clarify the ratio, but the chemistry behind a larger product mass is only partially explained.
clarity.evidence: No other reactant or source of added atoms appears in the observed explanation.

transfer.reason: The yield definition is generalized without a fresh reaction or calculation.
transfer.evidence: Only the same aspirin conversion and variable collected mass are explored.

accessibility.evidence: Keyboard, focus, contrast audit, phone, zoom/reflow and motion unknown.

surprise.reason: Matching the starting mass does not mean a full product yield.

visualExplanation.reason: The dashed possible-product bar provides the correct denominator visually.
visualExplanation.evidence: Input, theoretical product and actual product share a clear scale.

playfulness.reason: The interaction is a guided calculation rather than a puzzle toy.
playfulness.evidence: Two stage buttons and a mass slider expose the calculation.

practicalValue.reason: It clarifies the meaning of percent yield.
practicalValue.evidence: Yield compares collected product with theoretical product, not unlike reactant mass.

depth.reason: The calculation is explained, while reaction stoichiometry is assumed.
depth.evidence: The one-to-one mole relation is used without the full chemical reaction.

complexity.reason: Moles, molar masses and stoichiometric conversion are substantial prerequisites for the everyday learner boundary.
complexity.conceptualDemand: High: distinguish masses of different substances and compare amounts before converting back.
complexity.interfaceBurden: Low: two conversion buttons, slider and target preset.
complexity.conceptualChallenge: The theoretical mass of a different molecule is the relevant yield denominator.
complexity.prerequisiteNovelty: Moles, molar mass and one-to-one stoichiometry are introduced or assumed.
complexity.notationRepresentationBurden: High: decimal mass values, grams per mole and chained unit conversions.

whyCool: A product can weigh more than the starting powder at full yield, so the obvious mass ratio measures the wrong thing.
caveat: The full reaction and other reagent supplying atoms are not shown in the observed explanation. This is a yield calculation, not a synthesis walkthrough.
missingEvidence: No fresh reaction, limiting reagent or full reaction equation was tested.
